# Salla Sutta (Snp 3.8 (PTS Snp 112))

**ID:** Snp 3.8 (PTS Snp 112)
**Section:** Suttanipāta (snp)
**Collection:** Suttas-Early-2
**Title (Pali):** Salla Sutta
**Title (English, SuttaCentral):** The Dart
**SuttaCentral:** https://suttacentral.net/snp3.8

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Salla Sutta* ("The Dart", also translated as "the shaft of grief") is the eighth discourse of the *Mahāvagga*, the third chapter of the *Suttanipāta* (Snp 3.8, PTS Snp 112) [Anderson and Smith 1913; Khosla 1989; SuttaCentral; Sarada Thero, Treasury of Truth]. The sutta presents an exposition on the nature of mortality, declaring that while physical decay, old age, and death are unavoidable for all living beings—young and old, wise and foolish alike—grief and lamentation are unnecessary and detrimental [Bond, Death Meditation; Khosla 1989; SuttaCentral; Sarada Thero, Treasury of Truth]. Employing vivid poetic similes, the Buddha compares mortals to ripe fruits that constantly face the danger of falling in the early morning [Gjellerup 1999; Sarada Thero, Treasury of Truth]. The text instructs the wise person to extract the internal dart (*salla*) of sorrow, longing, and grief to attain tranquility and peace of mind [SuttaCentral; Sarada Thero, Treasury of Truth].

Verses of the *Salla Sutta* are widely shared and cited across Buddhist literature. Both SuttaCentral and DharmaNexus verify extensive Pali text reuse between this sutta and the *Dasarathajātaka* (Ja 461) as well as the *Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā*, with additional parallels attested in the *Mūgapakkhajātaka* (Ja 538) [SuttaCentral; DharmaNexus]. Canonical and post-canonical Pali reuse is also documented in the *Jarāsuttaniddesa* of the *Mahāniddesa* (Mnd 6), the *Sappurisa Sutta* (MN 113), the *Suttanipāta-aṭṭhakathā*, and the *Nīti-gantha-saṅgaho Caturārakkhadīpanī* [SuttaCentral; DharmaNexus]. Beyond Pali, SuttaCentral lists verse parallels in the Gāndhārī Dharmapadas (G-Dhp and G3-Dhp), the Sanskrit *Udānavarga* (UV 1), and several Chinese translations of the *Dharmapada* (T 210, T 212, and T 213) [SuttaCentral]. DharmaNexus additionally aligns segments of the text with the Tibetan *Vinayavastu* (D0001-2), the Chinese *Ekottarika-āgama* (T 125), and the Sanskrit *Patna Dharmapada* [DharmaNexus]. In the manuscript tradition, the text also circulated independently; the PTS editors noted an independent Siamese manuscript in Cambodian script containing only the *Salla-Sutta*, preserved in Copenhagen [Anderson and Smith 1913].
